paragraphs: The bus left me at a [[petrol]] station on the edge of the village, and the school was only a [[distant]] white shape on the hillside. I [[intended|intend]] to stay six weeks and help my aunt, who had [[founded|found]] the place twenty years earlier. She pointed me to the [[restroom]] behind the kitchen and then to a [[tent]] pitched on the [[lawn]]. The tent was for me, she said, because every room inside was full of children.

The school was [[affordable]] for families who could pay almost nothing, and its [[dropout]] rate had fallen to zero. Every morning began with [[physical]] exercise, and the children ran with an [[endurance]] that shamed me. My aunt was [[respected|respect]] by every child, and she gave the same [[respect]] to the slowest runner. Her [[colleague]] Mr. Tan taught maths and kept the accounts, [[apart]] from the two years he had spent in the city.

The school's [[infrastructure]] was [[fragile]]: one pump, one generator, and a kitchen roof that would [[crumble]] in a strong wind. I spent my first week helping to [[mow]] the [[lawn]] and pull [[weed]]s from the [[garden]]. The garden fed the youngest children, so a morning of weeding was not a small thing. The shed behind the kitchen held tools that no one had bothered to [[classify]] for years.

On Monday my aunt [[appointed|appoint]] me to teach English to the oldest class. She [[assigned|assign]] me forty students and a [[schedule]] that began at six. Before I could stand in front of them, I had to [[apply]] for a temporary teaching permit. The [[enrollment]] list was handwritten, and I [[classified|classify]] the children by reading level. One boy, the class [[monitor]], was a [[special]] case: he could not hear well and needed [[precise]] instructions. A new [[type]] of lesson was needed for him, one with pictures and fewer words.

In July a [[turbulent]] storm broke over the valley, and the rain was so [[intense]] that the road became a stream. The generator died, and in the [[disorder]] that followed nobody could find the candles. A small [[avalanche]] of mud blocked the lower path, and three children were [[interrupted|interrupted]] on their way home. We [[extinguished|extinguish]] the kitchen fire with wet sacks and spent the night in the hall. The [[tension]] only lifted at dawn, when everyone had [[survived|survive]]. The storm's [[depredation]] was everywhere: torn roofs, broken fences, a hillside stripped of grass.

It took a month to [[restore]] the pump and reopen the road. We had to [[allay]] the children's fear of hunger, though nobody actually [[starved|starve]]. A [[lever]] and a rope moved the fallen beams, and the new classroom came to [[resemble]] the old one so closely that the children laughed. The stone walls were still [[intact]], [[moreover]], which saved us a fortune. A cheap [[outlet]] in the county town [[undercut]] local prices, and two volunteers came to [[assist]] with the buying.

The rebuilding needed money, so my aunt [[pledged|pledge]] her savings and asked the village for help. A [[sponsor]] from the city offered to pay for a new roof, but only with the council's [[approval]]. The council agreed and began to [[distribute]] the funds in stages. A tax [[incentive]] was meant to [[compel]] absent landowners to contribute, and families that lost crops were [[compensated|compensate]]. Every household had a [[stake]] in the result, which is why the work went so fast.

Then a [[commercial]] company announced a dam upstream, and the village found itself in a [[conflict]] it had not chosen. The company's [[scheme]] would divert the river that fed our pump. Our lawyer argued that the [[federal]] [[constitution]] protected the village's water, and that the [[jurisdiction]] belonged to the provincial court. There was no [[precedent]] for such a case, and a [[prosecution]] of the company seemed unlikely. I helped [[investigate]] the company's records, and a [[drumbeat]] of questions followed every meeting.

On clear nights an [[astronomer]] from the city set up a telescope and used a red lamp to [[illuminate]] the star chart. He showed the children the [[spectrum]] of a distant star and explained that its colours reveal what the star is made of. One girl asked whether [[astrology]] could predict the rains; he said the two only [[coincide]] by accident. That night was a [[reflection]] on how little we know, and my [[intuition]] told me the girl would become a scientist. The school kept a small [[exhibit]] of her drawings in the corridor.

My aunt and I had an [[intimate]] talk on the roof, the kind we had never managed in the city. She was [[conscious]] of her age and [[concerned|concern]] about who would run the school after her. I tried to [[express]] my fears without sounding ungrateful. Her answer was [[explicit]]: she would stay until a successor was ready, and she [[assured|assure]] me that the village would help. She warned me against the [[superiority]] of city people, and against the [[gap]] I had begun to feel between two lives. What she said left a [[profound]] impression on me.

The children put on a [[drama]] about the flood, written in three days and entirely [[spontaneous]]. They [[aspired|aspire]] to things I had stopped imagining: a clinic, a library, a bus that came twice a day. Their parents [[possessed|possess]] little money but spoke of a future [[prosperity]] no one in the city would have predicted. The play ended with a [[tragic]] scene, and the whole hall went silent.

There was a fine [[irony]] in it: the dam builders were [[extravagant]] in their promises and absent when the rain came. The land dispute was an [[inherited]] quarrel, older than the school itself, and no one [[risked|risk]] a direct accusation. The company's men had [[aggressively]] repeated that the dam would bring work to everyone. A [[pregnant]] woman in the front row laughed and cried at once, and the performance [[attracted|attract]] parents who had never come before.

I tried a new [[approach]] to science: we [[explored|explore]] the stream with nets and jars. The [[diverse]] life in one pool [[astounded|astound]] the class. I asked them to [[specify]] what they saw and to [[address]] one question at a time. An [[array]] of beetles, snails and tiny fish covered the table.

The children [[assimilated|assimilate]] new words faster than I could write them down. A [[dynamic]] classroom, I learned, is one where the teacher moves and the children [[dominate]] the discussion. Physics was the [[dynamical]] part of the day: wheels, weights, and a wooden cart.

In August the court [[declined|decline]] the company's request and refused to [[exclude]] the village from the hearing. The company had tried to [[intimidate]] witnesses, which only [[stimulated|stimulate]] the village to organise. The ruling [[promoted|promote]] a new idea: water belongs to the people who live beside it. We began to [[conserve]] the spring and to [[prolong]] the life of the old pump. The school's success [[consisted|consist]] of small things: a repaired roof, a full classroom, a promise kept. To [[avail]] ourselves of the new funds, we had to [[construct]] a proper store room and [[stick]] to the plan.

The summer had been a small [[revolution]] in how I thought about work. I began to [[recognise|recognise]] how much I had changed, and the children seemed to [[recognize|recognize]] it too. I learned to [[communicate]] without translation and to [[connect]] a family's story with the river. My aunt would [[mention]] a name, then [[confer]] with the oldest woman in the room before telling the rest. One [[aspect]] of village life surprised me: no one [[attempted|attempt]] to hide a quarrel.

At dinner we ate rice from tin [[plate]]s in the yard. My aunt [[fulfilled|fulfil]] her promise to train a successor, and the council promised to [[fulfill|fulfill]] its part by winter. The school had once had a high [[turnover]] of staff, but she had engineered a [[turnaround]] in two years. She [[resisted|resist]] every attempt to [[restrict]] its intake and refused to [[dismiss]] a child for poor marks. She could [[apprehend]] a child's trouble before the child said a word, and she [[tackled|tackle]] each problem like a [[pragmatist]].

On my last morning I tried to [[compose]] a song for the children and failed; they sang their own instead. The school had taught me that [[anthropology]] begins at home, not in a distant archive. I was [[averse]] to leaving, and a [[plastic]] chair on the lawn was the last thing I saw from the bus. The village had become an [[asset]] in my life rather than a subject of study. I could not [[reverse]] the decision to go, or [[invert]] the order of that summer, so I promised to return. Their songs would [[propagate]] through the valley long after the bus had gone, and I would [[confront]] the city with what I had learned.
